one_liner: This paper demonstrates that using identity mappings as skip connections and moving activation functions before convolutional layers (pre-activation) significantly improves training stability and performance in extremely deep ResNets.
paragraphs: Deep residual networks (ResNets) revolutionized deep learning by enabling training of very deep neural networks through skip connections that bypass layers, but the original design used ReLU and batch normalization after the addition operation (post-activation). This paper investigates why this design works well and identifies that the key to stable training lies in preserving clean, direct signal paths—both forward and backward—through the network. The authors argue that non-identity skip connections (like scaling or 1x1 convolutions) and post-activation operations disrupt these paths, leading to harder optimization and poorer convergence in ultra-deep networks.

To address this, the authors propose a new residual unit design that enforces two identity mappings: (1) an identity skip connection (h(x) = x), and (2) making the activation function f(y) also an identity by moving batch normalization and ReLU before the weight layers (pre-activation). This allows gradients to flow directly back through skip connections without being altered by nonlinearities or normalization, and ensures that the output of a residual unit is simply the input plus a learned residual function. The mathematical analysis shows that this structure enables direct propagation of signals across many layers, preventing gradient vanishing and simplifying optimization.

Experiments show that the proposed pre-activation ResNet achieves state-of-the-art results on CIFAR-10 (4.62% error with 1001 layers) and CIFAR-100, outperforming the original ResNet design which struggled with training stability beyond 100 layers. On ImageNet, a 200-layer pre-activation ResNet achieved better performance than the original 152-layer version without overfitting. These results prove that depth can be further exploited with proper signal flow design, and the pre-activation structure has since become standard in modern deep networks due to its improved trainability and generalization.
key_takeaways: Identity skip connections are critical for maintaining clean signal propagation in deep networks.
Moving batch normalization and ReLU before convolutional layers (pre-activation) improves training stability and performance.
Pre-activation ResNets enable training of much deeper networks (e.g., 1001 layers) without degradation in performance.
Gradient signals are preserved better with identity mappings, preventing vanishing gradients even in very deep architectures.
The original post-activation design is suboptimal for ultra-deep networks, and pre-activation is a superior alternative.
eli5: Imagine you're building a super long slide with many bumps and obstacles. The old way made kids climb up, then go down, then climb again—each time getting slower. The new way lets kids just slide straight through with a smooth path, and only add tiny fun bumps (the learning part) along the way. This way, even if the slide is super long, kids don’t get tired and still reach the bottom fast!
prerequisites: Familiarity with residual connections and backpropagation
applications: Training ultra-deep CNNs for high-accuracy image recognition in medical imaging and autonomous vehicles
Designing scalable deep learning models for video analysis and satellite imagery processing
title: Identity Mappings in ResNets
